data.title: UP amends tourism policy to promote budget hotels, homestays and rest stops
data.description:
With domestic and international tourist arrivals rising in Uttar Pradesh, the state government has amended its tourism policy to extend incentives and relaxations to hotels, homestays and rest stops.
 
Under the revised policy, hotels with as few as six rooms will now qualify as budget hotels. Earlier, a minimum of 10 rooms was required. Hotels with six to 49 rooms, each with an attached bathroom, will now fall under the budget hotel category. The policy has also been relaxed to facilitate the development of rest stops along highways in the state.
 
The state Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, approved amendments to the Uttar Pradesh Tourism Policy, 2022. The changes will enable smaller hotel operators to avail themselves of benefits under the policy and are also aimed at promoting rural tourism, farm stays, traditional cuisine, local handicrafts and cultural tourism.
 
 
Tourism and culture minister Jaiveer Singh said the amendments would help create an investment-friendly environment and give emerging tourist destinations in the state a distinct identity.
 
Under the revised norms for budget hotels, establishments will need to have commercial and goods and services tax (GST) registrations and comply with prescribed building regulations. Eligible hotel operators will be able to apply for incentives available under the tourism policy, extending its benefits to smaller businesses.
 
The amended policy also recognises permissible sub-leases on land owned by government bodies for the development of highway rest stops. Eligible operators will be able to avail themselves of policy benefits subject to prescribed conditions, registration and consent of the landowner.
 
However, the stamp duty exemption will be available only once for an eligible transaction. If the original lessee has already availed itself of the benefit, the sub-lessee will not be entitled to claim it again.
 
Provisions relating to homestays and bed-and-breakfast units in rural and urban areas have also been aligned with the state’s 2025 policy and subsequent amendments. The framework provides for approvals within one month and registration through the UP Tourism portal.
 
Registered units will continue to be treated as residential buildings, receive electricity and water at domestic tariffs, and get marketing support from the tourism department.
 
To showcase Uttar Pradesh’s local culture and heritage, ‘Parampara’ Heritage Experience Centres will be eligible for benefits under the cultural centre category of the tourism policy.
 
At these centres, tourists will be able to sample regional cuisine, buy handicrafts and One District One Product (ODOP) items, and learn about local folklore and cultural traditions. Tourism-related information will also be available at the centres.
 
The revised policy also seeks to integrate the state’s culinary traditions more closely with tourism. Traditional eateries and culinary heritage will be identified and promoted, while food trails and culinary festivals will be organised to popularise regional cuisine.
 
The initiative is also expected to strengthen the One District One Cuisine (ODOC) campaign, helping give traditional dishes greater visibility and develop local cuisine as a tourism attraction.
 
To expand rural tourism, activities linked to agriculture, animal husbandry and local cuisine will also be promoted. Visits to gaushalas, dairy production units, and groups engaged in natural and organic farming could form part of the tourism experience.
 
Natural and organic farming have also been explicitly included within farm-stay activities. This is expected to provide farmers with opportunities to earn additional income from tourism alongside agricultural activities.

data.title: Gold, silver prices fall amid stronger dollar, hawkish Fed signals
data.description:
Gold and silver prices remained under heavy selling pressure on Friday, November 20, as the US dollar strengthened and expectations of further interest-rate increases by the Federal Reserve intensified.
 
Several Federal Reserve officials have backed higher interest rates to bring inflation closer to the 2 per cent target. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has also indicated the possibility of a 50-basis-point increase in December.
 
At the time of writing, gold futures on Comex were trading near $3,550 per ounce, while silver was trading near $41.80 per ounce.
 
In the domestic market, gold futures on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) were trading near ₹1,23,000 per 10 gram, while silver futures were trading near ₹1,49,600 per kg.
 

Gold prices fall sharply

Gold futures opened sharply lower. On the MCX, the benchmark December gold contract opened ₹3,823 lower at ₹1,23,629 per 10 gram. The previous close was ₹1,27,452.
 
At the time of writing, the contract was trading ₹4,373 lower at ₹1,23,079.
 
Gold futures had touched a high of ₹1,59,700 per 10 gram earlier this year.

Silver also tumbles

Silver futures also opened sharply lower. On the MCX, the benchmark December silver contract opened ₹6,299 lower at ₹1,51,183 per kg. The previous close was ₹1,57,482.
 
At the time of writing, the contract was trading ₹7,880 lower at ₹1,49,602.
 
Silver futures had touched a high of ₹4,20,048 per kg earlier this year.

Gold, silver weak in global market

Gold and silver were trading sharply lower in the international market.
 
On Comex, gold opened at $3,633.80 per ounce. The previous closing price was $3,685.50. At the time of writing, it was trading $132.30 lower at $3,553.20 per ounce.
 
Gold prices had touched a high of $5,586.20 per ounce earlier this year.
 
Comex silver futures opened at $42.86 per ounce. The previous closing price was $44.35. At the time of writing, silver was trading $2.52 lower at $41.83 per ounce.
 
Silver prices had touched a high of $121.79 per ounce earlier this year.

Why are gold and silver falling?

Vikram Subburaj, chief executive officer of Giottus.com, said pressure on gold and silver had intensified as the dollar approached a 19-month high and expectations grew that the US Federal Reserve could raise interest rates in December.
 
Analysts said forced selling by investors had also accelerated the decline. The impact of the international sell-off was visible in the Indian market as well, with domestic bullion prices falling sharply.

Levels to watch

According to Ajay Kedia, director, Kedia Advisory, gold was technically witnessing long unwinding. Open interest fell 9.78 per cent to 11,952 contracts, while prices declined by ₹2,362, indicating that investors were exiting existing long positions.
 
The technical data placed support at ₹1,26,500, followed by ₹1,25,540. However, the current gold price quoted in the report, at ₹1,23,079, is already below both support levels.
 
Resistance is seen at ₹1,29,100. If gold sustains above this level, prices could recover towards ₹1,30,750.
 
Silver was also technically witnessing long unwinding. Open interest declined 9.9 per cent to 15,308 contracts, while prices fell by ₹3,252, indicating that investors were exiting existing long positions.
 
The technical data placed support at ₹1,55,340, followed by ₹1,53,200. However, the current silver price quoted in the report, at ₹1,49,602, is already below both support levels.
 
Resistance is seen at ₹1,60,900. If silver sustains above this level, prices could recover towards ₹1,64,320.

data.title: India's energy demand to grow 3 times faster than global average: IEA
data.description:
The West Asia conflict has exposed vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains, with disruptions to key shipping routes raising concerns about the availability and cost of oil and gas. The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 examines how the duration of the crisis could shape global energy markets and influence countries' energy strategies.
 
The report also highlights India's growing energy needs, projecting that the country will account for more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region. Meeting this demand while ensuring reliable and affordable supplies will be a key challenge as India seeks to diversify its energy mix and reduce its exposure to external disruptions.
 
 

West Asia crisis shakes global energy markets

 
The scale of the disruption is reflected in the cumulative loss of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas from the Gulf since the crisis began, according to the IEA. By November 2026, the disruption to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz was still continuing, with the impact increasingly being passed on to consumers through higher prices as supply buffers ran down.
 
The pressure has been particularly severe in Asia, which accounted for around 80 per cent of the oil and nearly 90 per cent of the liquefied natural gas (LNG) that passed through the Strait before the crisis. Diesel supplies have also come under significant pressure, with prices crossing $200 per barrel.
 
The crisis is also prompting Gulf producers to reconsider their dependence on the Strait. According to the IEA, countries in the region are constructing or considering alternative pipeline projects with a combined capacity of around 7 million barrels per day. These projects could require investments of about $40 billion and add around $2 per barrel to export costs.
 
The IEA expects the disruption to have lasting implications for global energy trade, with countries increasingly looking to diversify suppliers, transport routes and energy sources. Solar power and nuclear energy could benefit from this shift, while faster electrification is emerging as another way to reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets.
 
For India, these changes carry particular significance. As one of the world's largest energy consumers and importers, the country faces the dual challenge of securing supplies amid geopolitical uncertainty and meeting rapidly rising domestic demand.
 

India's energy demand to surge

 
India is expected to record more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region, according to the IEA. The country's energy consumption is projected to grow by 2.5 per cent annually until 2035 under the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), around three times the global rate.
 
The increase will be driven by rising incomes, urbanisation, industrial expansion and growing demand for cooling and mobility. The IEA estimates that India will:
 
  • Add more than 12,000 cars to its roads every day over the next decade
  • See a 33 per cent increase in built-up spaces
  • Install an additional 200 million air conditioners in homes
  • Expand production of energy-intensive materials such as iron, steel and cement
 
This growth will put additional pressure on India's energy infrastructure and increase the need for reliable and affordable supplies.
 
However, India's dependence on imported fuels makes it particularly vulnerable to global disruptions. The country imports around 40 per cent of its overall energy requirements, including 90 per cent of its crude oil and 50 per cent of its natural gas.
 
The recent disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has highlighted this exposure, particularly for cooking gas. Around half of the LPG cylinders used by Indian households depend on supplies passing through the strategic waterway. LPG imports fell by more than 50 per cent during the first two months of the conflict, prompting the government to maximise domestic production and prioritise household supplies.
 

India's energy mix gets greener

 
Despite its growing energy requirements, India is making progress in diversifying its energy mix. Solar power accounted for half of the country's power capacity additions over the past decade, while India achieved its target of having 50 per cent of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
 
The IEA expects electricity demand to grow by 6 per cent annually over the next decade as transport, buildings and industries increasingly shift towards electricity.
 
Under the STEPS, India's electricity generation is projected to increase from 2,114 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 3,585 TWh by 2035. The share of non-fossil sources, including renewables and nuclear power, is expected to rise from around 28 per cent to 51 per cent over the same period.
 
However, coal will continue to play an important role in India's energy system because of its substantial domestic reserves. The IEA expects coal to increasingly provide flexibility to the power system as renewable energy capacity expands.
 

Dependence on imported fuels

 
India had nearly 6 million barrels per day (mb/d) of refining capacity in 2025, making it the world's fourth-largest country by refining capacity and third-largest by refinery runs. It is also the second-largest net crude oil importer after China.
 
With another 840,000 barrels per day of refining capacity under construction, India is expected to strengthen its role as an exporter of petroleum products, particularly diesel and other middle distillates.
 
However, the IEA projects that domestic crude oil production will decline by nearly 20 per cent by 2035 under the STEPS, while refining capacity expands by one million barrels per day. This will increase the country's overall crude import requirements, even as imports from West Asia remain broadly stable.
 
Cooking gas presents another challenge. India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, with domestic production meeting around 40 per cent of demand in 2025.
 
Under the STEPS, LPG demand is expected to grow by almost 400,000 barrels per day by 2035, while domestic supply increases by less than 100,000 barrels per day. Consequently, LPG imports could rise to nearly 1 million barrels per day.
 
The IEA also highlights a potential trade-off for refiners, as increasing LPG production could come at the expense of higher-value products such as diesel and petrol.
 

A faster shift to clean energy

 
The IEA's Additional Response Case (ARC) examines how faster adoption of clean energy, efficiency measures and domestic resources could reduce India's exposure to imported fuels.
 
Under this scenario, electric cars are adopted 30 per cent faster by 2035 than under the STEPS, while electrification and energy efficiency in industry accelerate. India could reduce its oil requirements by 580,000 barrels per day and natural gas consumption by 8 per cent compared with the STEPS by 2035.
 
This would also help bring LPG imports below 750,000 barrels per day, compared with nearly 1 million barrels per day under the STEPS.
 
The report suggests that faster electrification, greater use of renewables and improved energy efficiency could bring India closer to its ambition of achieving energy independence by 2047. However, the transition will require substantial investment in electricity infrastructure, domestic energy production and supply-chain diversification.

data.title: Nepal PM Balen Shah to visit India on November 22-23 at PM Modi's invite
data.description:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah will embark on a State visit to India from November 22 to 23 at the invitation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Nepal's Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai announced on Friday.

According to the Foreign Secretary, a 34-member government delegation led by Prime Minister Shah will depart from Kathmandu for New Delhi to undertake the high-level engagement.

During the visit, Prime Minister Shah is scheduled to hold a delegation-level meeting on Monday with his Indian counterpart, Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Following the delegation-level talks, the two Prime Ministers will jointly inaugurate various projects relating to energy, while bilateral instruments covering various aspects of cooperation will be signed and exchanged between the two sides.

 

After the delegation-level talks, Prime Minister Shah and Prime Minister Modi will also address a joint press conference, followed by a luncheon hosted by the Indian Prime Minister in honour of the visiting Nepali leader.

As part of his official itinerary in the national capital, Prime Minister Shah will call on President Droupadi Murmu during the visit.

The Nepali Prime Minister will also pay tributes and lay a wreath at the Mahatma Gandhi memorial at Rajghat, besides attending the Nepal-India Business Forum aimed at strengthening commercial and economic ties between the two countries.

Rooted in centuries-old historical, cultural, and geographical bonds, India-Nepal ties are underpinned by the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and a 1,751-kilometre open border. Commonly encapsulated by the traditional adage "Roti-Beti ka Rishta", symbolising shared livelihoods and familial connections, the bilateral relationship is now evolving towards pragmatic economic, energy, and digital integration under Nepal's new political leadership.

data.title: Paytm snaps 2-day losing run on S'pore investment plan; Nomura retains Buy
data.description:
Paytm share price target: Shares of Paytm parent One 97 Communications surged over 2.5 per cent in trade on Friday, snapping a two-session losing streak, after the company announced that its Singapore arm would invest up to ₹200 crore in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Societies, including about ₹162 crore for a 19.1 per cent stake in its payments subsidiary CardUp.
 
Paytm shares opened higher at ₹1,730 and extended gains to hit an intraday high of ₹1,770.30 on the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
 
In the previous two trading sessions, the stock had declined over 9 per cent amid reports that the proposed implementation of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions could be delayed further.
 
 
As the session progressed, Paytm shares pared most of their early gains. As of 11:35 AM, the stock was trading 0.45 per cent higher at ₹1,734 on the NSE.
 
Paytm shares have jumped 35 per cent in 2026 so far, compared with a 2.3 per cent decline in the Nifty 50 index. From 2026 low of ₹930.60, touched on March 30, the stock has bounced back over 85 per cent. The stock touched an all-time high of ₹1,960 on November 13. 
Paytm invests ₹200cr in funding societies, buys CardUp stake
 
According to a regulatory filing, the board of Paytm Singapore Pte Ltd on Thursday approved a partnership with Funding Asia Group Pte Ltd (Funding Societies). 
ALSO READ: Stock Market LIVE: Sensex at day's high, up 300 pts, Nifty reclaims 25,600; SMIDs trade mixed
 
The initial investment of about ₹162 crore will be made in cash for the issuance of shares in CardUp Pte Ltd, a payments subsidiary of Funding Societies. The remaining investment of about Rs₹38 crore may be made in one of Funding Societies' affiliates. Paytm expects the CardUp transaction to be completed by May 20, 2027.
 
One 97 Communications will also enter into a business and technology partnership with CardUp, under which it will provide payments and lending technology to the Singapore firm to expand Paytm's technology-led payments and financial services stack in Singapore. The company will receive technology fees and a revenue share under the agreement, which will be initially valid for five years with a right of renewal on mutually acceptable terms.
 
CardUp, incorporated in October 2015, is a Singapore-based digital payments company (a subsidiary of Funding Asia Group).  
Paytm share price target 
Following this, Nomura has maintained 'Buy' rating on Paytm stock, with a target price of ₹2,300. The target implies an upside of 33 per cent from the previous close of ₹1,725.90. 
 
The brokerage said that it expects Paytm to continue to target select international markets in a measured way, leveraging its proven technology stack in merchant payments and financial services.
 
Nomura believes that the investment is small relative to Paytm's balance sheet and is unlikely to change its financials materially in the near term. It is a low-cost way to enter the Singapore market.  
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: CEC appointment law: SC declines separate hearing to recall split verdict
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday declined a submission to separately list a plea seeking recall of a split verdict delivered by a two-judge bench on whether challenges to the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and Election Commissioners (ECs) should be referred to a larger bench.

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the recall application, as well as any challenge to the reference order, could be considered by the five-judge Constitution bench already constituted to hear the batch of petitions challenging the validity of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.

 

The CJI also said the five-judge bench could consider the recall application even after the retirement of one of the judges who delivered the split verdict.

Bhushan said that the recall application should be listed before the original bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma, which delivered the split verdict on September 23.

He pointed out that Justice Sharma was due to retire next week. Bhushan further said that Justice Sharma had a conflict of interest and, therefore, the application seeking recall of the verdict ought to be heard by the same bench.

When the CJI suggested that the reference bench could consider the application, Bhushan said the reference order itself was recalled on the ground of an alleged conflict of interest.

However, the CJI said that the issue could be raised before the five-judge Constitution bench, which has been constituted for final adjudication of the constitutional challenge to the 2023 law.

The development follows a split verdict delivered on September 23 by Justices Datta and Sharma on whether the petitions challenging the 2023 law warranted consideration by a larger bench.

The main objection was the exclusion of the CJI from the panel to select the CEC and ECs. The panel now includes the prime minister, the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and a cabinet minister.

While Justice Datta was of the view that the challenge could be adjudicated by a two-judge bench, Justice Sharma favoured a reference to a five-judge Constitution bench, considering the significant constitutional questions involved.

data.title: Indian space startup SatSure raises ₹60 crore from govt-backed space fund
data.description:
Indian space startup SatSure has raised ₹60 crore ($7 million) from a government-backed space technology ​fund as part of an ongoing ₹200 crore funding round, the company said on Friday.

The ‌investment comes as India seeks to expand its commercial space industry through reforms that have opened the traditionally state-dominated sector to private companies and investors.

The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund is investing at a post-money valuation of ₹870 crore ($93 million), SatSure said. The ₹1,600 crore fund is anchored by IN-SPACe, India's private space sector regulator, and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital, an arm of state-owned ‌small-business lender SIDBI.

Bengaluru-based SatSure uses satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to help banks, insurers, infrastructure firms and government agencies make decisions. Its subsidiary KaleidEO develops satellite imaging systems for Earth observation.

 

The series B round comprises ₹165 crore in fresh equity, ₹25 crore in venture debt and ₹10 crore in secondary transactions. The company expects to close the round by December ‌2026.

The proceeds will help prepare its satellite imaging payloads for launch in 2027, support its participation in ​India's ‌planned Earth-observation satellite network and expand its data analysis capabilities and ‌international operations.

SatSure's customers include HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, ITC, Bayer and the Airports Authority of India.

The startup has ‌raised ​₹427 crore ​from institutional investors, excluding grants, with previous backers including Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures and Asian ‌Development Bank ​Ventures.

data.title: Trading still anchors NSE's business as clearing section gains share
data.description:
NSE went public in September via an offer for sale, marking a significant milestone for the country’s largest stock exchange. Its results for the second quarter of the financial year (Q2 FY27), compared with the same period last year, show that its clearing services business grew faster than its dominant trading business in terms of revenue. Clearing revenue rose 13.74 per cent to ₹464.88 crore, against a 9.34 per cent increase in trading revenue to ₹3,603.99 crore. The “others” segment recorded the fastest growth of 32.54 per cent, taking its revenue to ₹211.95 crore. 
 
Trading’s profit surged 157.25 per cent to ₹2,496.21 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with ₹970.36 crore a year ago. The clearing services segment’s profit increased by just 3.34 per cent to ₹280.09 crore from ₹271.05 crore, while “others” grew 49.50 per cent to ₹117.28 crore. Despite clearing's faster revenue growth, trading continued to generate the bulk of segment profitability, with its result rising much more sharply during the quarter. 
 
Trading’s share of gross segment revenue (total segment revenue excluding revenue from other sources) declined from 85.29 per cent in Q2 FY26 to 84.19 per cent in Q2 FY27, while clearing’s share increased from 10.58 per cent to 10.86 per cent. “Others” also gained ground, with its revenue contribution rising from 4.14 per cent to 4.95 per cent. While trading remains overwhelmingly dominant, the rising contribution of clearing and other services suggests a gradual broadening of NSE’s revenue base.

data.title: Anthropic makes a $1.8 trillion debut: What investors should watch next
data.description:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has reached a new milestone. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, made its stock market debut on Thursday, in one of the biggest initial public offerings (IPOs) in history.
 
The company's shares closed at $97.17 apiece, 17 per cent above the IPO price of $83, giving it a fully diluted market value of $1.8 trillion. The strong debut made Anthropic the world's seventh most valuable company, placing it ahead of Saudi Aramco, Broadcom and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), Bloomberg reported.
 
Anthropic raised $81.3 billion through its IPO, surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest stock market offering on record. The company also raised another $26 billion through a separate private placement, taking the combined fundraising to about $107.3 billion.
 
 
However, the strong debut also puts the spotlight on questions about whether Anthropic can sustain its rapid growth, manage the high cost of developing AI models and turn its growing business into consistent profits.
 

What does Anthropic's performance tell us?

 
Anthropic's debut is being seen as a major test of investor confidence in the AI industry. The strong demand for its shares suggests that investors are still willing to put money into companies developing advanced AI models, despite concerns about high valuations and the cost of building the technology.
 
According to The Guardian, demand for Anthropic shares was about six times the number of shares the company offered. Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as “foaming at the mouth” for the offering, with allocations “impossibly low”, CNBC reported.
 
Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, told The Guardian, "The blockbuster Anthropic launch is a critical step in reassuring the market about the potential for AI, but it's really just the beginning."
 
He added that investors would need to watch developments at OpenAI, Nvidia, the political climate around data centres and Anthropic's performance over time before drawing conclusions about the stability of the industry.
 
Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, told CNBC that Anthropic's IPO was “exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment”, after weeks of negative sentiment around the AI sector.
 
However, US equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite declining 2.25 per cent, the S&P 500 falling 2.02 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average losing 2.19 per cent. James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers, told CNBC that the reversal in initial gains in AI and technology stocks to profit-taking across the sector. 
ALSO READ: Anthropic pares IPO gains as shares slide 5% in after-hours trading
 

What to watch after this public listing

 
One of the factors investors will monitor is Anthropic's ability to meet its growing computing requirements without putting further pressure on its finances.
 
The company has committed nearly $900 billion towards computing infrastructure, including data centres, according to its disclosures. These investments are essential to train and run advanced AI models but also expose the company to high long-term costs.
 
The Guardian reported that opposition to new data centres is also growing in parts of the US, with protests against projects and some local authorities considering restrictions. Any delay or regulatory hurdles in building new facilities could affect the availability of computing capacity needed by AI companies.
 
Investors will also be watching how Anthropic converts its technology into products and services that generate sustainable returns. Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CNBC that this would depend on the company's ability to expand enterprise adoption, improve its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services.
 

What does this mean for rival OpenAI?

 
Anthropic's successful listing could influence the plans of other AI companies looking to enter the public markets, particularly its biggest rival, OpenAI.
 
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has postponed its IPO plans until 2027. However, Anthropic's debut could offer an indication of how much demand there is among public-market investors for shares of companies developing advanced AI models.
 
Earlier this week, OpenAI Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Sam Altman said his company would go ahead with its IPO next year despite market volatility.
 
Altman commented on the strong demand for Anthropic shares, saying, "There's been way too much investor demand and not enough supply."
 
Walser told CNBC that Anthropic's listing was particularly important for the AI industry as it was the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public. The IPO gives public-market investors a chance to assess how a standalone AI model developer is valued, rather than judging the AI boom largely through chipmakers.
 

Can Anthropic sustain its revenue growth?

 
One of the biggest factors investors will watch is whether Anthropic can maintain the pace of revenue growth that helped it secure such a high valuation. Demand for its Claude AI models, particularly Claude Code, an AI-powered coding tool used by software developers, has been a major driver of its business.
 
According to the company's IPO filing, Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, 2026, up from $71 billion a month earlier. Its third-quarter revenue stood at $16.96 billion, marking a 47 per cent increase from the second quarter.
 
Its enterprise customer base has also expanded rapidly. Anthropic had 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of 2025.
 

Founder wealth and ownership structure

 
The listing has also created significant wealth for Anthropic's founders.
 
According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, the combined wealth of the company's seven co-founders rose to about $166 billion following the stock market debut. Each founder holds an estimated 1.3 per cent economic stake, putting their individual fortunes at around $24 billion.
 
However, the founders retain significant control over the company despite their relatively small individual stakes. A special Class F share held through Founder LLC carries 50.1 per cent of Anthropic's voting power.
 
The founders have also pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal equity in the company to philanthropic causes. However, these commitments are voluntary and can be withdrawn.
 

Can the $1.8 trillion valuation hold?

 
Anthropic's first trading session showed both strong investor interest and the possibility of sharp price movements.
 
The shares opened at $111.50, nearly 34 per cent above the IPO price, and briefly touched $114.99 before closing at $97.17. The closing price was still 17 per cent above the offer price.
 
There is also an important distinction between the company's market capitalisation and its fully diluted valuation. While its value based on outstanding shares was about $1.3 trillion, the fully diluted valuation, which includes stock options and other securities that could become shares, was approximately $1.8 trillion.
 
Analysts have cautioned investors against rushing to buy the stock after its strong debut. Walser told CNBC that investors should avoid “chasing the IPO”, while Morningstar's Khan said they should step back and carefully assess Anthropic as a long-term business.
 
Khan set a fair value estimate of $92 for the stock, below its first-day closing price. Walser, meanwhile, said the shares could come under pressure in the coming weeks, but that any weakness could offer an entry point for investors interested in the company over the long term.
 
The initial rally does not necessarily indicate how the stock will perform in the coming weeks. Investors will look at subsequent trading sessions, quarterly earnings, customer growth and spending trends to assess whether the valuation is supported by the company's business performance.

data.title: SatSure targets ₹200 cr in Series B to expand satellite and AI capabilities
data.description:
The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund (AVCF), backed by the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd (SVCL), is investing ₹60 crore in Bengaluru-based Earth-intelligence startup SatSure, leading the first close of its ₹200 crore Series B funding round.
 
The transaction marks AVCF's first investment in the downstream data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) layer of India's space economy, extending its investment footprint beyond launch and satellite hardware into commercial space-data infrastructure serving enterprise and sovereign markets.
 
“The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund is mandated to catalyse India’s private space ecosystem from proven technical capability to global commercial scale,” said Arup Kumar, managing director and chief executive officer of SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd.
 
 
“Leading SatSure’s Series B round reflects AVCF’s thesis of backing full-stack enterprises that pair indigenous orbital infrastructure with downstream decision intelligence. As India’s space economy matures, AVCF will continue deploying patient institutional growth capital behind space-tech companies built to compete internationally,” he said.
 
AVCF's investment will support four priorities for SatSure, in line with India's space commercialisation roadmap.
 
These include advancing its optical payloads ahead of a planned orbital flight in 2027 and executing a multi-satellite constellation mandate under the IN-SPACe-anchored Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership (EO-PPP).
 
The funding will also support the scaling of Dhaarini, SatSure's Large Earth Observation Model, which had earlier received a ₹24.6 crore grant under IN-SPACe's Technology Adoption Fund (TAF).
 
The company also plans to expand its international commercial operations from India.
 
SatSure's ongoing ₹200 crore Series B round comprises ₹165 crore in primary equity, ₹25 crore in venture debt and ₹10 crore in secondary transactions. The company expects to close the round on a rolling basis through December 2026.
 
Following the first close, SatSure's cumulative institutional capital raised stands at ₹427 crore, excluding government grants.
 
SatSure operates a full-stack Earth intelligence business through two entities.
 
Its subsidiary KaleidEO develops optical satellite payloads and builds complete satellites under India's Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership for the national Earth observation constellation.
 
SatSure, meanwhile, converts Earth observation data into decision intelligence for banks, insurers, critical infrastructure companies and governments.
 
Its operations span the value chain from satellite payloads and geospatial foundation models to AI, analytics and industry-specific applications.
 
“The strategic value of the space economy lies not only in reaching orbit, but in what we can understand from it. That intelligence is reliable only when you own the full chain behind it: from the payloads in orbit, to the AI and foundation models that turn that data into decisions enterprises and governments act on,” said Prateep Basu, chief executive officer and co-founder of SatSure.
 
“We built SatSure to own that full stack end-to-end, and the Series B round lets us build it further, from India, for the world,” he added.
 
SatSure's Earth intelligence technology is already integrated into India's financial infrastructure.
 
Its SatSource product line is part of the Reserve Bank of India's Unified Lending Interface (ULI).
 
Public-sector banks, including State Bank of India, use the platform to assess farm loan applications in minutes, a process that earlier took weeks, according to the company.
 
SatSure has 24 banking and financial services customers. These include HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, both of which are investors in as well as customers of the company.
 
SatSure's earlier funding rounds were backed by Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures, Asian Development Bank Ventures, Omidyar Network India, now Prana Ventures, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank and Nuvama Asset Management, among others.
 
India's space economy is projected to expand from around $8.4 billion in 2023 to $40-45 billion by 2030, according to a Jefferies report.
 
The government has set a target of building a $100 billion space economy by 2040.
 
The number of registered space startups in India has increased from one in 2014 to around 440 as of August 2026, according to government data.
 
Nine startups identified by Jefferies have collectively raised about $539 million, while cumulative private investment in the broader ecosystem reached nearly $600 million by FY26.
 
Among the leading companies, Skyroot Aerospace has raised $160 million, Pixxel $95 million, Agnikul Cosmos $76 million and Digantara $65 million.
